newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - HUNGARY ENERGY HIKE SEEN AS BLOW TO INVESTORS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - HUNGARY ENERGY HIKE SEEN AS BLOW TO INVESTORS.

text.p: Hungary's announcement on Thursday that it would hike consumer electric rates by 24.9 percent and gas rates by 18.8 percent in January was seen as a blow to investors expecting bigger increases.
But investors and analysts alike were reluctant to speak publicly about the long-awaited price hikes because many of the details were not revealed.
In announcing the broad outlines of the hikes, government spokesman Elemer Kiss told a news conference that a detailed analysis would be released later by the Ministry of Industry and Trade.

"Analysts are sitting here and screaming because people are calling them from all over the world saying, 'How much is it for MOL, how much is it for that?' And we don't know," one investment banker said, referring to the big state oil and gas concern which has been partly privatised.

Kiss in his announcement said only that state-owned energy companies were expected to get a four percent return on investment from the new rates, but he did not elaborate specifically on what the increase would be for MOL.
He added that the price increases would assure an eight percent profit margin for privatised energy companies, as the government had promised.
"Investors of course will regard the rates as too low," Kiss said.
"But according to my information I can say that they continue to think for the long term and they will accept this, even if not with great pleasure."

The increases were somewhat higher than what utility industry sources expected following a meeting on Wednesday between the government and representatives of companies that have bought large segments of Hungary's energy business.
At that time, sources said the government planned to hike rates by 23.5 percent for electricity and 16.4 percent for gas.
Despite the upward adjustment, analysts said it seemed unlikely that investors would get the eight percent return on investment they were looking for.
"These increases are way below inflation," one analyst said.
But some analysts agreed with Kiss that investors were unlikely to bolt because Hungary cut down the electricity rate hike by about 10 percentage points from what investors wanted.

"The German and French companies that have bought in here are here for the long term," one analyst said. "Americans who were looking for a quicker return on their money didn't come in the first place."
Kiss said the government felt justified in paring down the price increases.
"There are costs which only will be price factors in the future, but we do not exactly know when and to what extent. These should not be taken into account," he said.
He said the increases also should help the government meet its inflation target of some 18 percent average for next year.
"These rates are somewhat smaller than what the government took into account concerning with next year's inflation," he said.
